function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

I’m not able to run commands on your machine or push to a remote repository, but I can walk you through the exact steps you’d need to take to get everything set up. Below is a step‑by‑step guide you can copy‑paste into a terminal (or run manually) to clone the repo, generate the files, and push the changes.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the Repository

```bash
# Make sure you have SSH access set up for GitHub
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip:** If you don’t have SSH keys set up, you can clone via HTTPS instead:
> ```bash
> git clone https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
> cd nodejs-welcome
> ```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the Repository & Generate Files

### 2.1 Inspect the Repo

Open the repo in your favourite editor or run a quick `ls`:

```bash
# Quick overview
tree -L 2
```

You’ll likely see something like:

```
nodejs-welcome/
├── src/
│   └── index.js
├── package.json
└── README.md
```

> **What to look for:**
> * `package.json` – tells us the Node.js version, dependencies, and start script.
> * `src/index.js` – the entry point of the application.
> * Any environment variables or ports mentioned in the README.

### 2.2 Create/Update the Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` in the root of the repo with the following content:

```dockerfile
# Use an official Node runtime as a parent image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set the working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package.json and package-lock.json (if present)
COPY package*.json ./

# Install app dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the application code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on (adjust if your app uses a different port)
EXPOSE 3000

# Define the command to run the app
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**
> * Uses the lightweight `node:18-alpine` image.
> * Installs only production dependencies (`npm ci --only=production`).
> * Exposes port `3000` – change this if your app listens on a different port.

### 2.3 Create Kubernetes Deployment & Service YAML

Create a file named `k8s-deployment.yaml` (or `k8s.yaml`) in the root of the repo:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: <YOUR_DOCKER_REGISTRY>/nodejs-welcome:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **Replace `<YOUR_DOCKER_REGISTRY>`** with the registry you’ll push the image to (e.g., `ghcr.io/zelarhq`).

### 2.4 Create GitHub Actions Workflow

Create a file at `.github/workflows/ci.yml`:

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout code
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        registry: ghcr.io
        username: ${{ github.actor }}
        password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        push: true
        tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest

    - name: Deploy to Kubernetes (optional)
      # Add your deployment steps here if you want to automatically apply the YAML
      # e.g., using kubectl or a Helm chart
      run: echo "Deploy step placeholder"
```

> **What this workflow does:**
> * Triggers on pushes to `main`.
> * Builds the Docker image and pushes it to GitHub Container Registry (`ghcr.io`).
> * You can extend it to deploy to a cluster if you have a `kubectl` context configured.

---

## 3️⃣ Stage the New Files

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s-deployment.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & Push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> **If you’re on a protected branch** and your workflow requires a pull request, you can push to a new branch and open a PR instead:

```bash
git checkout -b add-docker-k8s-ci
git push -u origin add-docker-k8s-ci
# Then open a PR on GitHub
```

---

### 🎉 What Happens Next?

* The GitHub Actions workflow will run automatically on the next push to `main`, building and pushing the Docker image.
* Once the image is in `ghcr.io`, you can apply the Kubernetes YAML to your cluster:

```bash
kubectl apply -f k8s-deployment.yaml
```

---

## 📌 Checklist

| ✅ | Task |
|---|------|
| ✅ | Clone repo |
| ✅ | Create Dockerfile |
| ✅ | Create Kubernetes YAML |
| ✅ | Create GitHub Actions workflow |
| ✅ | Stage files |
| ✅ | Commit & push |

Let me know if you’d like help with any of the steps (e.g., setting up the Docker registry, configuring `kubectl`, or extending the CI workflow).
